rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Lamb Is Wanted
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a grand lady in a horse-drawn carriage holding up a laughing baby boy, five children in straw hats racing down a country lane after the carriage, dust rising, a policeman running, golden afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The very next morning the children ran down to the gravel pit and dug until they found the Psammead. He was sitting up out of the gravel, with his snail eyes on stalks. "Well?" he said crossly. "What is it to be today? Some new way of getting into trouble?" "Nothing could go wrong with this one," said Anthea. "I wish the Lamb may be wanted by everybody who sees him."
Everybody wants to hold the Lamb - and a grand lady carries him off in her carriage.

At first it was lovely. Everyone who saw the baby smiled and wanted to hold him. Strangers in the lane stopped to play with him and to stroke his little golden head. It seemed the safest wish they had ever made. The children began to feel very proud of their clever wish.

Then a grand lady came driving down the lane in a beautiful carriage. It was drawn by two shining horses, with a coachman and a footman behind. She stopped. She looked at the Lamb. "Oh, what a darling baby!" she cried. And before the children could say a word, she had lifted the Lamb into the carriage. The carriage rolled away down the road, faster and faster.

The children raced after the carriage, through the lanes and over the stiles, calling and crying. The carriage rolled on and on, and the Lamb's little voice grew faint. Then a kind policeman came running up the road. He blew his whistle and held up his hand, and the carriage stopped at the crossroads at last.
New word: carriage - a fine, horse-drawn coach with soft seats, in which rich people rode.

Just then the sun went down - and the wish went with it. The grand lady looked at the baby in her arms as if she had never seen him before. She set him down quickly on the grass and drove off, wondering what she had been doing. Anthea caught the Lamb up and hugged him till he squeaked. "We shall never wish anything about the Lamb again," she said. "Never, never, never. Nobody but us is going to be allowed to want our baby."

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · A Castle and No Dinner
chapters.artPrompt: five children and a baby standing in the stone courtyard of a great medieval castle, tall towers with banners flying against a grey rainy sky, a drawbridge over a dark moat, empty stone kitchens behind them, cold grey light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One wet, dreary afternoon the children sat looking out at the rain. "I wish," said Robert at last, "that we were in a castle - a real one, like in the story-books. It must have a moat, and a drawbridge, and flags on the towers." They dug out the Psammead, and he blew himself out, and the wish was made.

The rain was still falling - but it was not their rain. They were standing in a great stone courtyard, with tall towers overhead and banners flying against the grey sky. A drawbridge crossed a wide, dark moat, and a portcullis hung above the gate like a great iron jaw. It was exactly like a story-book castle. It was almost too exactly.
The children stand in the courtyard of a great stone castle - with no dinner anywhere.

For a whole hour it was wonderful. They climbed the wall-walks and looked out at the winding river. They peeped into the great hall, with its long tables and its banners. Then Cyril's tummy gave a loud rumble, and everyone thought of dinner. And that was when they found out that there was no dinner in a wished-for castle at all.

The kitchen was all stone, with a fire that no one had lit. There was no cook, no bread, no milk, not even a crust. There were fat hens walking about the courtyard, but the hens were much too quick. And the drawbridge was up, and the moat was deep, and there were no shops in the Middle Ages.
Question for you: The children asked for a castle, and they got one. Why was being hungry in a castle much worse than being hungry at home?

So they sat on the wall-walk and waited for sunset, hungrier and hungrier. The Lamb cried until Anthea sang to him. The shadows grew long, and the wind came up cold from the moat. When the sun sank low, the towers grew dark, and the whole castle melted away like mist in the rain. They were standing on their own wet lawn. They ran in and ate bread and jam by the fire. And the plainest bread in the world never tasted half so good.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Siege?
chapters.artPrompt: armoured men climbing long wooden ladders against the grey stone walls of a castle, arrows flying over a courtyard, five children and a baby crouching behind stone battlements with a wicker basket, dramatic stormy light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The next day the children went back to the gravel pit, and wished themselves into the castle again. This time they were not so silly. They took a basket with them, packed with bread and apples and a bottle of milk. "A castle without a dinner," said Robert, "shall not catch us twice."

But when they arrived, the castle was not quiet at all. There were men on the walls, and horns blowing, and a great shouting from beyond the moat. Armoured men were climbing up the outer wall on long ladders, and arrows came whistling over the courtyard. A drum began to beat somewhere behind the walls. It was a siege.
Armoured men raise long ladders against the castle walls while arrows whistle overhead.

The children crouched behind the battlements with the Lamb, and their hearts went knock, knock, knock. The castle's own men pushed the ladders down, and the attackers splashed into the moat. Was it real, or was it some old game? Nobody stopped to tell them, and there was no one to ask.
New word: siege - when an army surrounds a castle and tries to break in and take it.

They ate their bread and apples in a corner of the wall. Even plain bread was good when your heart was thumping. The Lamb, who was too little to be frightened, laughed at the horns and clapped his hands. "I wish we knew how it ends," whispered Jane. "We shan't know," said Anthea. "We shan't be here."

And she was right. When the sun went down, the walls, the banners and the horns all faded like breath off a window. The children stood safe on their own lawn in the evening light. The basket was still on Cyril's arm. They never did find out how that siege ended. And the older ones agreed that some things are better not to know.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Bigger than the Baker's Boy
chapters.artPrompt: a baby boy grown into a friendly giant taller than a cherry tree, crowing and clapping enormous hands, five children in straw hats tugging at his sleeves and pulling him back down a country lane, a startled baker's boy with a bread basket, bright summer light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: A few days later the baker's boy came down the lane with the bread. He was in one of his cross moods. He made rude jokes about the baby, and laughed, and would not say he was sorry. Robert went red all over. He marched straight off to the gravel pit. "I wish," he said, "that the Lamb was bigger than the baker's boy!"
The Lamb, grown into a giant taller than the cherry tree, plays catch with his laughing brothers and sisters.

The Psammead blew himself out - and the Lamb began to grow. He grew past the baker's boy in a moment. He grew past the baker. He grew past the tallest man in the village, and past the top of the garden wall. At last he stood a great giant of a boy, taller than the cherry tree. He laughed down at them all.

But a giant baby is a very difficult thing. He was still a baby inside, and he wanted to play. He crowed, and clapped his enormous hands, and wanted to play catch. And when he tottered down the lane toward the village, the children ran round him. They pulled and tugged and begged him to stop. But you cannot tell a giant what to do.

They coaxed him up the lane, and they coaxed him down the lane. At last they coaxed him to the gravel pit. "Please make him little again," cried Anthea. "Oh, please - before he steps on the church!" The Psammead blew himself out, and the Lamb grew smaller and smaller. At last he lay laughing in Anthea's arms, a proper baby again.
New word: giant - a person far, far bigger than anyone else. The Lamb was one, just for one afternoon.

"Never again," said Robert, wiping his hot face. "We shall never wish anything for the Lamb - except that he stays exactly as he is." "That," said the Psammead grumpily, "is the first sensible thing any of you have said all summer." And he went to sleep in the gravel with his snail eyes shut.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Last Wish
chapters.artPrompt: a small brown furry creature with bat ears and snail eyes sinking into sunlit gravel, five children standing hand in hand around the pit in the quiet evening light, long shadows, first stars appearing, soft golden dusk, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The summer was ending. The leaves were turning, and Father and Mother would be home in a few days. The children went down to the gravel pit one more time, and dug out the Psammead. He looked smaller and thinner and very tired, like a toy left out in the rain.

"This is the last wish," he said quietly. "I am going to sleep now for a long, long time. So think carefully, and make it a good one." The children looked at each other. Wings had left them stuck on a tower. Beauty had made them strangers. Gold had made them robbers. The castle had starved them. And the Lamb, grown giant for an afternoon, had nearly walked into the village.
The Psammead sinks into the gravel like a stone into water, and the pit is still.

"What we really want," said Anthea slowly, "is that Father and Mother may never know about you. Never, never, all their lives. Then nobody can ever catch you, or put you in a cage. And nobody can make you grant wishes to people who don't deserve them."
New word: content - quietly happy with what you have, without wishing for anything more.

The Psammead smiled. It was the first time they had ever seen him smile, and it quite changed his funny old face. "That," he said, "is the best wish you have made all summer - and the last." Then he sank slowly into the gravel, like a stone sinking into water, and the pit was still.

A day or two later Father and Mother came home. The white house was full of talking and laughter again. Nobody ever knew about the Psammead. But the children often went to look at the gravel pit. Sometimes they smiled at each other for no reason at all. They had had their wishes. And they had learned that the nicest things of all are the things you never need to wish for.
